item.title: Fleeing the U.S. and Torn Apart: Family Separation at the Northern Border
item.description:
In the dead of night, a rental car sped north from Springfield, Ohio, toward the Canadian border. Inside were a mother, a father, their two toddlers and some hastily packed pieces of the American life they were leaving behind.

For over three years, the young couple, Keyla François and Noelson Pierre, had worked, started a family and planned their future in the United States. But panic took hold in early August, after the Trump administration terminated deportation protections for more than 300,000 Haitians and federal agents began rounding up families.

“We were terrified of being taken from our children,” said Ms. François, 30.

The couple believed they could seek asylum in Canada, a country that currently doesn’t deport Haitians and where Mr. Pierre, 30, had two brothers with lawful status. But they encountered unexpected barriers. Because Ms. François did not have immediate relatives of her own in Canada, she was barred from entering.

Their hope for a fresh start ended in the very nightmare they had tried to avoid: family separation. Today, Ms. François is locked inside an immigration detention center in New Mexico, 2,000 miles away from Mr. Pierre and their toddlers, ages 1 and 2, in Montreal. It remains unclear when, or if, she will be reunited with them.

More than 1,300 people, many of them Haitian, were turned away at the northern border between Jan. 1 and Nov. 16 because Canadian officials determined that they were ineligible to enter under the Canada-U.S. Safe Third Country Agreement. The treaty prohibits people from seeking asylum in Canada if they are entering from the United States, based on the premise that they could secure protection there first.

An exception is made for people with a spouse or close relative in Canada, and many Haitians with family members north of the border have used that to seek asylum. But the exception does not apply to in-laws. In cases where a couple have both filed for asylum in the United States, each spouse needs their own close relative in Canada to gain admission.

There is no official tracking of how many families seeking refuge in Canada have been separated, but The New York Times interviewed lawyers aware of dozens of such cases. Child welfare officials in Quebec, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to talk to the media, described a spike in unaccompanied minors crossing the border.

“We are witnessing families forced to make heartbreaking choices between family unity and the safety of their kids every day at the border,” said Anne Cécile Khouri-Raphael, a Montreal-based immigration lawyer who has advised dozens of separated families.

Lawyers, immigrant advocates and Canadian officials described three separation scenarios unfolding at the border. A parent allowed to enter Canada proceeds with the children while leaving the other parent behind; a single parent denied entry sends their children without them; or parents send their children to the border alone, knowing officials won’t turn away minors.

“The reality of family separation at the border largely remains invisible,” said Jenn McIntyre, coordinator for the Canada-U.S. Border Rights Clinic, a nonprofit.

Many of the Haitian children whose families have tried to cross into Canada had acclimated to the United States after fleeing killings, kidnappings and systemic violence in Haiti, only to be uprooted again, this time without a parent. Some have been shuffled between caregivers, often relatives they had never met before, Canadian officials said.

Citing the bilateral agreement, the Canadian Border Services Agency said it “does not separate families who arrive together at the Canadian border.”

“The family has the option to return together to the United States to preserve the family unit,” said Rebecca Purdy, an agency spokeswoman. “Otherwise, the eligible family members may choose to proceed into Canada, knowing that this will result in separation.”

In a statement, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said Immigration and Customs Enforcement had arrested Ms. Francois, who was returned to the United States by Canadian border authorities.

Ms. François and Mr. Pierre arrived in Springfield in March 2023, after crossing the southern border with an appointment secured through a Biden-era program. They followed friends to the small Ohio city, where logistics and manufacturing jobs had lured thousands of Haitians eager to work.

Granted protected status and work permits, the couple found jobs at an Amazon distribution center in nearby West Jefferson. They saved, bought a used car for $10,000, and in 2024, welcomed their first child, Jackson. Soon after, they moved into a three-bedroom duplex with a patio and an expansive, grassy front lawn.

“We were prospering in Springfield,” said Ms. François in an interview from a detention center in Texas in September.

Their landlord, Levenson Laguerre, echoed that sentiment, describing the couple as model tenants who unfailingly paid their $1,200 monthly rent on time.

In 2025, they welcomed their second child, Micaela.

Their stability began to unravel when the Trump administration announced it would eliminate Temporary Protected Status for Haiti. A legal battle ensued to preserve it, but the Supreme Court ruled in late June that the administration had authority to terminate it. The safeguard ended in July, placing hundreds of thousands of Haitians at risk of detention and deportation.

The end of T.P.S. for Haitians is among several measures taken by the Trump administration to overhaul the U.S. immigration system. It has also suspended access to asylum at the border, canceled humanitarian parole programs and largely shut down the U.S. refugee program, except to white South Africans and a very small number from other countries. The changes have coincided with a push to deport one million immigrants per year.

The crackdown has prompted legal action in Canada challenging whether the United States can still be considered a “safe third country” for people seeking refuge under the bilateral border treaty.

Stéphanie Valois, another lawyer in Montreal, questioned how Canada could return Haitians to the United States, effectively facilitating their deportation to Haiti, which Canada itself has halted removals to because of the country’s perilous state.

“There is no misunderstanding here about conditions in Haiti,” she said, adding, “It’s impossible to believe Canada would do this.”

Many families were unaware of the risk of separation when they approached the U.S.-Canada border.

One of Ms. Valois’s clients, a 47-year-old Haitian man named Jules, sought refuge in Canada in August with his wife and two children after losing their protected status. Jules’s brother is a Canadian citizen.

After a two-day taxi ride from Florida to the New York-Quebec border with their daughters, ages 3 and 4, Jules and his wife presented their documents to Canadian officers. They were fingerprinted and photographed. Hours later, officers said Jules’s wife didn’t qualify for entry.

Sitting in an isolated booth at a fast food eatery in Saint-Jerome, 30 miles northwest of Montreal, Jules wept as he recounted the day and the aftermath. He spoke on the condition that his last name be withheld out of concern for his wife’s safety.

His wife was turned away and immediately taken into U.S. custody. Over 40 days, she bounced between four detention centers. Then, on Sept. 24, following an asylum hearing, she was deported to Haiti. She is currently in hiding; her family’s home outside Port-au-Prince has been seized by gangs.

A woman named Cassous said that her twin girls had been thriving in the United States since the family fled Haiti in 2022 to escape the violence that erupted after the assassination of the president. Her husband remained in Haiti while she and her girls, who were 9 when they fled, received T.P.S.

When the Trump administration announced it would end the protection, she decided their best option was to join her husband’s sister in Montreal.

“Leaving Haiti was traumatic enough. I wanted to spare my daughters living in fear in the U.S.,” she said in an interview punctuated by sobs. She spoke on condition that only her first name be used to avoid being targeted for arrest by federal agents.

After overnighting in a Canadian border facility, officers informed them that only the twins could enter. The mother decided to send the girls without her.

They have struggled to adjust, she said, and have already relocated from their aunt’s home to live with another relative.

U.S. authorities did not detain Cassous after Canadian officers returned her because T.P.S. for Haitians had not yet expired. Now stripped of her protection and right to work, she can no longer send her daughters money. She dreads being deported to Haiti and moving further away from her daughters.

After T.P.S. for Haitians was revoked this summer, federal agents descended on Springfield, arresting people outside their homes, at gas stations and on the streets. Terrified that she and her husband could be swept up, Ms. François called their landlord to tell him they might need to break their lease.

Days later, they were gone. All that remained of the family were a portable crib crammed with discarded belongings by the curb and an overturned toy, an empty car-seat box and a passport size photo of a baby on the porch.

On the evening of Aug. 17, the family embarked on the 700-mile journey toward Champlain, N.Y., praying the cover of darkness would shield them from highway officers who could hand them over to ICE.

At the station in Lacolle, Quebec, the family presented their Haitian passports, the children’s U.S. passports and proof that Mr. Pierre had two brothers living in Montreal, just 40 miles away.

Officers informed them that while Mr. Pierre and the children could enter, Ms. François was ineligible.

“I pleaded, ‘Please let me go with my children,’” Ms. François recalled telling the officers through tears. “‘We are fleeing.’’’

When Canadian officers held firm, the couple said they would rather return to the United States. “We thought we would go free,” recalled Mr. Pierre in an interview.

Instead, Canadian officials turned them back, and U.S. border authorities locked them in a facility in Champlain, the couple said in separate interviews.

For several days, they remained in limbo. Mr. Pierre, confined to a men’s section, was permitted just 20 minutes a day with his wife and children. When the toddlers contracted severe diarrhea, Ms. François feared that her 1-year-old daughter was becoming dangerously weak.

One night, officers produced a “voluntary departure” form, seeking their consent to be deported to Haiti. The couple declined to sign, they said, arguing that this would put their children in harm’s way.

Officers responded with an ultimatum, Ms. François and Mr. Pierre said. If they refused deportation, they would be transferred to ICE detention centers in the interior of the country and their children would be removed from them.

Unwilling to risk losing their children to the state, the couple decided to surrender Ms. François’s freedom. D.H.S. did not comment on the terms the officers presented to the couple.

On Aug. 28, U.S. authorities drove Mr. Pierre and the toddlers back to the border.

They had no idea how narrowly they had escaped deportation. Their names had appeared on the manifest, obtained by The Times, for a flight that expelled other Haitian families days earlier.

Today, Mr. Pierre and his children are physically safe in Montreal. Yet he is consumed by worry for his wife as he struggles to care for the toddlers and settle into a new country.

Ms. François was issued an exclusion order that bans her from entering Canada for one year. But she’s unlikely to be admitted until her husband gets lawful status, which could take years.

She has passed through four detention facilities in four different states.

On Sept. 20, she vanished from the detainee locator.

“I am looking for her in the system and I can’t find her,” said Mr. Pierre. “I don’t know what they did with her. Do you think they deported her?”

Several hours later, her name reappeared at a facility in New Mexico, where she remains.

Hamed Aleaziz contributed reporting and Sheelagh McNeill contributed research.

item.title: MAGA Attacked Harvard. So Harvard Taught a Class About It.
item.description:
Harvard University may have never tangled with an adversary as relentless as the Make America Great Again movement.

The Trump administration, the governing arm of MAGA, has threatened Harvard’s research grants and its ability to host international students. It has sued Harvard in a hunt for admissions documents, and accused the university of discrimination. The 400-year-old institution has been forced to fend off one attack after another in court, Whac-a-Mole style.

How does an institution of elite academics process that level of ill will?

They study it in class.

Harvard’s John F. Kennedy School of Government this fall offered its first for-credit course on the MAGA phenomenon.

The class was not to evangelize students for or against MAGA, but to understand it, by diving into the literary canon of an anti-establishment movement that “hates Mitt Romney as much as Hillary Clinton,” said Stephen Richer, who led the class.

Mr. Richer is a fellow at the Cato Institute, a libertarian public policy group, and a former Republican elected official in Arizona. He sees MAGA as “the most consequential political movement of the 21st century,” for its role in U.S. politics and government, and the right-of-center populist imitators it has influenced in other countries.

“Make America Great Again: The Ideas Behind the Movement” was a half-semester course that attracted about 50 students. The class was a follow-up to a more informal study group Mr. Richer led last year on the topic.

The class explored some of the big questions that surround MAGA, such as: Is it a coherent political ideology? Or just a hodgepodge of President Trump’s policy preferences?

The MAGA class recently finished, just as many American voters signaled that they, in fact, might be finished with MAGA: Voters overwhelmingly favored Democrats in the midterm election, heightening the question about what happens to the MAGA movement when Mr. Trump is out from office.

“I don’t think the ideas are going away,” Mr. Richer said after the election.

For Harvard, one of President Trump’s favorite targets as he and his administration have pushed a populist overhaul of American society, the future of MAGA may be fundamental to the university’s own future, too. It has lost millions in federal research funds, laid off hundreds of workers , and was hit with union strikes.

Mr. Richer’s class was not the only one at Harvard studying how recent political tumult has affected the university itself. Former Harvard President Claudine Gay, a member of the faculty who lost her leadership role in early 2024, amid campus upheaval related to the war in Gaza along with allegations of plagiarism against her, is teaching a course called, “What is a University?” A goal of the class is to get Harvard students to think critically about their own school.

Mr. Richer, 41, has seen MAGA’s animosity first hand. In 2020, he was elected as a Republican to the office of Maricopa County Recorder, a post that oversees voter registration and early voting for Arizona’s most populous county. He lost his position in a GOP primary four years later, after resisting baseless MAGA-fueled claims that the 2020 election was stolen.

Readings in MAGA class opened with “The Flight 93 Election,” a 2016 essay by political writer Michael Anton that characterized the 2016 election between Mr. Trump and Mrs. Clinton in apocalyptic terms. The class also studied Mr. Trump’s 2017 inaugural address, known as the “American carnage” speech for its dark depiction of a broken nation, along with writings and speeches from other figures under the MAGA umbrella, including Vice President JD Vance and Steve Bannon.

Matt Cook, a student in the class, said that one of the more provocative reading assignments was by Bronze Age Pervert, the pseudonym for a right-wing author and internet personality. Selections from the author sparked a vivid class discussion about the educational merit of writing that many found crude and homophobic, said Mr. Cook, 28, who is from the United Kingdom.

“There were people saying, ‘This is hate speech, it shouldn’t be on the reading list,’ ” he said. “And others saying, ‘We’ve got to have the freedom to engage with these things. This is part of the canon.’ ”

Mr. Cook said he found the selection unpleasant, but saw value in engaging in the full spectrum of political thought.

MAGA’s attacks on higher education have always been laced with the notion that universities had become hostile to conservative thinking. In that sense, the very existence of a class aimed at rigorously studying the movement’s ideas might be considered a win.

Isha Bodas, 27, who is pursuing a masters in public policy at the Kennedy School, said she took the class to engage with different political perspectives.

Ms. Bodas has spent much of her life in liberal places, including Seattle, Chicago, and New York.

Studying “the strongest versions” of MAGA political arguments didn’t reorder her views, she said, but it did force her to become more rigorous in her own political thinking.

You usually don’t have to defend your politics, she said, “when you’re surrounded with people who generally agree with you, as I have been before coming to Harvard.”

item.title: Win in Tennessee Gives Democrats Largest House Majority in 3 Decades
item.description:
Democrats picked up their 259th seat in the House on Tuesday, as their victory in a largely rural district in Tennessee gave them their largest majority in three decades.

Victoria Broderick, a progressive tech support worker who ran for the House as a Democrat, narrowly defeated Representative Scott DesJarlais, according to The Associated Press, unseating an eight-term Republican in one of the biggest upsets this cycle.

Her victory in Tennessee’s Fourth Congressional District will give the Democrats their biggest majority since the early 1990s, when the party held 267 seats. In the largest House majority on record, Democrats won 334 seats in 1936. Republicans won their largest House majority, 302 seats, in 1920.

A few House races were not yet called as of Tuesday, including Minnesota’s First District, which will advance to a recount on Nov. 30, and Louisiana’s Fifth and Sixth Districts, where runoff elections are scheduled in December. In all three districts, which Mr. Trump won, Democrats were leading overall by a slim margin.

Ms. Broderick’s victory was one of the most striking upsets by Democrats in the midterms in part because many election forecasters had rated her race as solidly Republican. President Trump had won the Fourth District by 24 points in 2024, making it the constituency most strongly aligned with Mr. Trump that Democrats have taken so far. And Mr. DesJarlais defeated Ms. Broderick by 43 points just two years ago.

She had also been outspent by a vast margin. Her campaign spent just over $90,000, compared with $508,000 spent by Mr. DesJarlais, according to Federal Election Commission data. Her campaign had no record of airing a television ad.

“I just sat there in just disbelief,” Ms. Broderick said in an interview published the week after Election Day, when she led Mr. DesJarlais by fewer than 300 votes. “It was surreal.”

Ms. Broderick became the only Democrat in Tennessee’s new congressional delegation. Republicans had carved up the state’s congressional map after a Supreme Court decision weakened the Voting Rights Act of 1965, in an effort to sweep all nine House districts, including a reliably Democratic one that had included Memphis. The new boundaries added part of Nashville and neighboring Rutherford County to her district, making it lean less Republican than before.

Before the race was formally called, Mr. DesJarlais said in a statement on Nov. 16 that he had conceded to Ms. Broderick. “All of us hope that the new Member of Congress feels the same level of awe and gratitude for this tremendous undertaking that I felt every day I had the privilege of serving,” he wrote.

Ms. Broderick, 34, was born in Brandon, Fla., and lived in several places in the South, including in San Antonio and Atlanta, before her family moved to Tennessee in 2007, she said in an interview. She said she was involved with the Democratic Party in high school, but her experience of a miscarriage in 2021 helped deepen her political activism.

The failure of her intrauterine device, or IUD, led her to discover that she was pregnant, she said. Ms. Broderick had to navigate the medical care system, and then miscarried, which she described as an education in the physical challenges of a pregnancy.

About a month later, she said, she became pregnant again. While she was on maternity leave after having her baby, the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade. That decision, she said, compelled her to act.

“I can’t stand by anymore,” she recalled thinking. “I have to do more.”

She began talking about politics on TikTok and became a chairwoman of the Lincoln County Democratic Party. In 2024, she ran for Congress.

She said throughout her recent campaign that she supported abortion rights, along with progressive policies like Medicare for all, a proposal for universal government-funded health insurance. She also identifies as a member of the L.G.B.T.Q. community.

She said that her campaign, which also focused on affordability and reducing inequality, was informed by her experience in the service industry.

“This wasn’t a right or left fight for me,” she said. “This was a bottom versus top.”

Ms. Broderick defeated Mr. DesJarlais by less than one point, or about 270 votes out of more than 195,000 cast.

“We did not have the political machine behind us,” she wrote on social media on Nov. 4, the day after Election Day. “We didn’t have corporate PAC money, we didn’t have powerful insiders. We had you, the people.”

That day, Ms. Broderick said, she told her boss she needed the day off because she might have been elected to Congress. The next day, she wrote in a statement: “This win is a testament to the fact that working class people, people just like you, have a place in deciding your today and your tomorrow.”

item.title: Account Funding Trump’s D.C. Makeover Got $300 Million Boost
item.description:
In September, a government bank account that President Trump has used to help fund his makeover of Washington received a $300 million infusion. No one will say where it came from.

Government documents reviewed by The New York Times show that about $300 million in additional money was deposited that month into a National Park Service account that has collected funds for the president’s passion projects.

The financial reports do not identify the source of the money, nor the projects it would finance. The Trump administration also declined to answer questions about the money.

The bank account that received the funds was originally set up to collect donations for national parks around the country. But since Mr. Trump returned to office, he has funneled it toward his vision of a much grander, golder Washington — raising money from his political allies and from companies, some of which want something from his government.

The result has been a flood of money, much of it from undisclosed sources.

The bank account, which had previously received less than $100 million per year, has now taken in about $790 million since Mr. Trump returned to office last year, according to government reports. Mr. Trump has tapped it to pay for projects like the construction of the White House ballroom, the repairs to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, and — more recently — design work on the president’s planned triumphal arch.

Even in that context, the money given in September stood out — both because of the size and because government reports indicate that it was much larger than the National Park Service anticipated. The influx of money in September has not been previously reported. The records do not show if the money came from a single source, or several sources.

A spokeswoman for the Interior Department, which oversees the Park Service, did not provide details about the money. Instead, the spokeswoman, Katie Martin, gave a broader statement praising Mr. Trump and his work to remake Washington.

“President Donald J. Trump has done more to make our nation’s capital a shining beacon than any other president in the history of this country,” Ms. Martin said.

The Times was alerted to this new infusion of cash by Tony Irish, a longtime Interior Department lawyer who now works as senior counsel for a watchdog group, Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility.

Mr. Irish said he was stunned at the size of the donated funds, and the apparent secrecy with which they had been raised.

Last year, by contrast, Mr. Trump had embarked on a high-profile campaign to raise money for the ballroom, including hosting a White House dinner in which he recognized major donors. The Times reported last year that the White House agreed to keep some donors’ identities secret, arguing that there was no legal requirement to disclose them.

The result of that fund-raising campaign was roughly $330 million in commitments from donors, according to a list obtained by The Washington Post.

This year, Mr. Irish said, the administration appeared to have raised nearly the same amount again, without any public notice. The documents show no sign that the Interior Department was expecting donations at that level. The agency said it anticipated $50 million in donations to this account in September, but received $347 million that month instead.

Because of that secrecy, Mr. Irish said it was impossible to determine if these donated funds had created conflicts of interest within the Trump administration.

“Are the donors seeking certain government benefits?” Mr. Irish said. “We just don’t know, because of the lack of transparency.”

This new money could help Mr. Trump carry out his vision for Washington even if Congress’s new Democratic leaders next year seek to cut off the taxpayer funding he has used to supplement the donations. The administration has also used entrance fees from parks around the country to pay for his projects in Washington.

But it is difficult to know how much of Mr. Trump’s vision he could build with $300 million in new funding, in part because judges have blocked several of the projects temporarily, and in part because the Trump administration has said little about what it all will cost.

The Times has estimated that the full price tag will be more than $1 billion, but the total cost of the projects, including the arch, remains unknown.

Andrea Fuller contributed reporting.

item.title: Unstoppable Crowds Are Meeting Up to Push Immovable Objects
item.description:
Let’s say you have decided to try to move something that weighed hundreds of tons or more. Doing this by yourself might be difficult. So, you seek the help of as many strangers as you can assemble.

One might think the response would be lackluster.

But incredibly, in recent weeks, strangers have been showing up across the country to join with others, motivated perhaps as much by whimsy as altruism, to try to move immovable objects.

It started on Nov. 8 at Cloud Gate, the 110-ton public sculpture in Chicago’s Millennium Park that most know as the Bean.

Hundreds of people turned up to move the Bean, as reported by Art News. They were responding to anonymous fliers posted in person and circulated online suggesting that it was vital to move the Bean. A webpage suggested that moving the Bean would expose a hidden door and help a man trapped inside.

“If we move the bean about seven inches to the left,” it claimed. “We might be able to access that door and give the man inside the Bean resources.”

Result: The Bean did not move.

Civic rivalry seemed to be a motivator for a similar effort a week later at the 630-foot-tall Gateway Arch in St. Louis. It weighs a lot more than the Bean.

Megan Estopare, who promotes her home city with the website StlAin’tBad, came up with the idea after hearing of the Bean-push.

“It started as a joke,” she said in an interview, “but it gained a lot of traction.”

“We get a lot of bad media every time St. Louis is mentioned,” she said. “I thought it would be exciting to to have the city get together for something silly and harmless.”

“Chicago couldn’t do it,” Kyle Mrotek, one of the pushers, told St. Louis Public Radio. “We got to show them up. Show them the better city — it’s us.”

Dozens wound up pushing against the arch, again hoping to move it an arbitrary seven inches. “Everyone who showed up was leaning into it as a joke,” Ms. Estapore said, “yelling, ‘Put your back into it.’”

Result: The arch did not move.

New Yorkers, never liking to be left out, organized an effort to push their own arch-shaped landmark, in Washington Square Park, on Saturday. A couple dozen people showed up in a lighthearted mood, ready to push, and document the effort on social media.

Result: This 73½-foot-tall arch, too, did not move.

At a time when the president is making fairly significant alterations to the capital, residents on Sunday decided for a tweak of their own: pushing the Washington Monument.

Organizers had noticed that while the monument was more or less aligned with the Lincoln Memorial on an East-West line, it was a bit farther off a North-South line with the White House. The pushers said they hoped for a better configuration.

Thirty or so people showed up.

“It’s just fun to bring people together and bring people actually out to the monuments,” one participant told News9, “I think if you live here, you kind of forget that this is here.”

Result: The monument did not move.

There is nothing new under the sun.

In 1967, during an antiwar March on the Pentagon, the Beat poet Allen Ginsberg got the idea to try to to levitate the headquarters of the Defense Department. The Yippies Abbie Hoffman and Jerry Rubin joined with Ginsberg in the attempt.

After speeches near the Lincoln Memorial, tens of thousands began crossing the Memorial Bridge into Virginia and toward the Pentagon, which the protesters saw as the center of the Vietnam War that they fiercely opposed.

“There was no plan about what to do when we got to the building,” the activist Bill Zimmerman recalled in 2017. “The more whimsical spoke of ‘levitating’ the building and ‘exorcising’ the evil spirits inside.”

They were not enough people to circle the Pentagon, one of the world’s largest office buildings which has 17-1/2 miles of corridors. Still, there was chanting and willpower. And a lot of what the organizers were looking for was news media attention, which they got.

Result: The Pentagon did not levitate.

But for Ginsberg, that did not matter.

“The levitation of the Pentagon was a happening that demystified the authority of the military,” he told Smithsonian Magazine in 2017. “The Pentagon was symbolically levitated in people’s minds in the sense that it lost its authority, which had been unquestioned and unchallenged until then.”

item.title: U.S. Spy Agencies Suffer Breach of Some Unclassified Information
item.description:
The Central Intelligence Agency and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence recently discovered a cybersecurity breach that exposed some of their unclassified information, according to U.S. officials and other people familiar with the matter.

The intrusions affected an open-source intelligence analysis system, a computer network that looks for intelligence insights in public, unclassified material, the people familiar with the issues said.

It was not clear specifically what information was compromised, but classified material was not jeopardized, the people said. Information at other government agencies was also believed to have been exposed in the breach, according to two of the people.

Open-source intelligence can include vast troves of commercially available data sets, social media content, satellite imagery and other online material. Much of it is publicly available, but it can include information sold by data vendors that can be highly revealing, especially when combined with other tranches of data.

Spy agencies can also use the data alongside other sources of intelligence to inform analytical judgments.

It is not uncommon for federal agencies to suffer cybersecurity breaches, but several have recently detected intrusions into some of their systems, prompting heightened concern among current and former U.S. intelligence officials.

The officials and others familiar with the matter spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss a sensitive security matter that had not been made public.

The C.I.A. declined to comment. The Office of the Director of National Intelligence did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The episode coincides with a surge of technological disruptions, including a dayslong outage last week of the National Security Agency’s internal classified network that officials and businesses said were not the result of cyberattacks. The problems have rattled the American public. U.S. officials say that in some cases, artificial intelligence is uncovering software vulnerabilities that need to be quickly patched.

In this instance, it appears that a hacker gained unauthorized access to at least one government system, though the people familiar with the matter did not say whether investigators knew who was responsible.

It is just the most recent breach of government systems to surface recently. Last week, President Trump appeared to confirm that the F.B.I.’s National Crime Information Center — a nationwide database used to swap information among local, state and federal law enforcement agencies about criminal suspects — had recently been hacked.

“I will say that it’s not good — I don’t like that,” Mr. Trump said on Saturday during a phone interview with Fox News when asked about the F.B.I. breach, which CNN had reported earlier. The F.B.I. is investigating the breach, according to people familiar with the matter.

Also last week, the U.S. Department of Agriculture discovered a cybersecurity incident that led to some of its internal applications being taken offline, according to a department employee. News of the U.S.D.A. matter was reported earlier by Nextgov, a site that focuses on federal government technology issues.

Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, whom Mr. Trump recently tapped as his acting cyber director, appeared on several news programs on Sunday trying to quell rising public anxieties about recent technology outages, including the national air grounding earlier this month. Officials have said the flight issues were caused by issues related to router maintenance.

Pressed on the recent hack of the F.B.I. crime database, Mr. Clayton said breaches occurred frequently and that there was no cause for alarm.

“Cyberprobing, cyberincidents, they have been part of the American economy, part of the American life for a long time,” Mr. Clayton said on ABC’s “This Week.”

“And what we’re hearing about the F.B.I., and what I’ve talked to them about is, they have an incident. They’re dealing with it in the ordinary course.”

Glenn Thrush contributed reporting.

item.title: Trump Awards Giuliani the Presidential Medal of Freedom
item.description:
President Trump on Tuesday awarded his longtime ally Rudolph W. Giuliani, the famed mayor of New York turned infamous election denier, the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

Mr. Trump promised last year to bestow the medal, considered the nation’s highest civilian honor, on Mr. Giuliani, 82. In that announcement, which came just days after Mr. Giuliani was in a car accident. Mr. Trump called him the “greatest Mayor in the history of New York City, and an equally great American Patriot.”

The ceremony was not public, but Mr. Giuliani posted pictures on social media of himself wearing the medal in the Oval Office, as he celebrated the honor with his family and the president. In a statement, he wrote that he was “honored and humbled” to receive the medal.

“I share the credit with all the men and women who worked with me, disagreed with me, and loved me — particularly those who lost their lives in the causes we undertook together,” Mr. Giuliani wrote.

“Doing the right thing for others has been my guiding light,” he added.

Mr. Giuliani rose to prominence as a crime-fighting prosecutor in New York City, where he gained recognition for taking on organized crime in the 1980s, and then as the mayor who led the city through the Sept. 11 attacks. He became a symbol of leadership and resilience and garnered the unofficial title of “America’s mayor.”

But his profile has been tarnished in the course of his long affiliation with Mr. Trump.

Mr. Giuliani became one of Mr. Trump’s most trusted advisers during Mr. Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign and served as his lawyer during his first term. After Mr. Trump lost the 2020 election, Mr. Giuliani propagated the president’s false claims that the election had been stolen. Federal investigators included him as a co-conspirator in the case accusing Mr. Trump of plotting to overturn the 2020 election results.

Mr. Giuliani was also found to have defamed election workers in Georgia and was indicted along with others in Arizona for trying to overturn the state’s election results in 2020 in Mr. Trump’s favor. Like the federal election prosecution of Mr. Trump, that case has since been withdrawn.

But after being charged, Mr. Giuliani was disbarred in New York and Washington, D.C. He also settled with two Georgia election workers after they won a $148 million judgment against him for repeatedly making false statements against them.

In an interview after the ceremony, Mr. Giuliani’s son, Andrew Giuliani, told reporters that it was an “unbelievable honor” to watch his father receive the medal at the ceremony, which he said was attended by family and friends. He said Mr. Trump had spoken fondly about his relationship with the former mayor, which had endured for more than 40 years.

“I think there are incredible parallels too between the two of them,” the younger Mr. Giuliani said. “As I think about what my generation and younger generations can learn from President Trump and from Mayor Giuliani — perseverance.”

He also defended his father’s choice to support Mr. Trump in the ill-fated quest to challenge the results of the 2020 election.

“I think what Rudy Giuliani has done over the last six years will go down in history as one of the most important legal jobs that has ever been done by any attorney to defend the president of the United States against some of the evil forces that were out there,” he said.

The Presidential Medal of Freedom, established by President John F. Kennedy in 1963, is bestowed by a sitting president at his discretion. Fewer than 700 have been awarded.

Mr. Trump has often used the honor to reward his political allies, a practice not unknown to previous presidents. He has also shown a particular affinity for sports figures, bestowing the honor on Babe Ruth, Tiger Woods, Roger Staubach and Annika Sorenstam, among others.

Ali Watkins contributed reporting.

item.title: Officials Dismiss Rental Car Felony Charge for Incoming House Democrat
item.description:
A county prosecutor in North Carolina said on Tuesday that he had dismissed a felony charge against Representative-elect LaKesha Womack in a 2019 case about an unreturned rental vehicle.

Law enforcement officers had served Ms. Womack a criminal summons at a campaign rally in October, six years after the charge was filed and just weeks before the election.

News of the charge shadowed Ms. Womack, a Democrat, in the waning weeks of her bid to unseat Representative Tim Moore, a Republican.

After Ms. Womack defeated Mr. Moore, who had helped craft the gerrymandered U.S. House district he ran in, the rental vehicle charge continued to be part of the story of her win, which was one of many unexpected outcomes in North Carolina in the midterms. Mr. Moore had used the charge in ads attacking his opponent.

Spencer B. Merriweather III, the district attorney of Mecklenburg County, N.C., which includes Charlotte, said in a statement that the charge was dismissed after Ms. Womack paid what the rental company said were overdue fees for the days she kept the car beyond the rental agreement. Mr. Merriweather did not say how much Ms. Womack paid to the company, Budget Car Rental.

The car dealer also told the district attorney’s office that “the corporation did not wish to proceed further with prosecution and considered the matter resolved,” Mr. Merriweather said.

Budget did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Ms. Womack, who worked as a business consultant for entrepreneurs, previously said in an interview that she did not have permanent housing when she moved to the Charlotte area with her son in 2017. A medical emergency caused her to fall into financial hardship, she said, and they lived in a hotel as she struggled to get an apartment.

Ms. Womack rented the vehicle in August 2019 and renewed it two times; the third and final rental period began in October 2019. Law enforcement recovered it undamaged in December 2019 and returned it to the dealer, according to Mr. Merriweather. A criminal summons for failure to return hired property, a felony, was issued against Ms. Womack on Jan. 14, 2020. That summons was not served.

Ms. Womack was unaware of the original summons, according to her lawyer, Harold Cogdell Jr.

A summons was reissued and served by law enforcement on Oct. 11 while Ms. Womack was at a campaign rally. It is unclear why such a long period of time had elapsed before a summons was reissued.

Last month, Ms. Womack told The Charlotte Observer that she would “hate to believe that this was brought forward to give my opponent an unfair advantage by implying I’m a felon.”

Mr. Moore did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Ms. Womack had far fewer resources for her campaign than her opponent, raising just $56,000 to Mr. Moore’s $2 million. She ran on attaining funding for rural hospitals, supporting affordable housing development and raising the federal minimum wage.

item.title: Blanche Downplays Questions Over Nvidia as Company’s Customers Come Under Scrutiny
item.description:
Attorney General Todd Blanche on Tuesday dismissed mounting questions about Nvidia’s possible exposure to criminal charges, publicly blessing the company as a “good corporate citizen.”

His remarks, made at a news conference, came even as Justice Department investigators have gathered evidence on two separate fronts of the company’s high-powered computer chips being illegally diverted by other firms to China, according to people familiar with the inquiries.

His comments suggested the administration had no evidence that the company was a witting participant in any diversion of A.I. technology to China, despite the fact that investigators are pushing forward with cases against Nvidia’s customers in Asia, including a woman, seen by U.S. officials as an asset of Chinese intelligence, with whom the company’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, has acknowledged having an affair.

President Trump has similarly all but exonerated Mr. Huang of any wrongdoing, even though investigations into the diversion of the chips remain in progress. The president said on Monday that there was no evidence that Mr. Huang had broken the law, an assertion repeated by Mr. Blanche on Tuesday.

“I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen,” Mr. Blanche declared, adding that the F.B.I. had found no evidence of criminal wrongdoing by Mr. Huang.

“To the extent that the Department of Justice had information that he was committing crimes or something like this, that is something I certainly would have told the president, had it been true,” Mr. Blanche said.

Mr. Huang has come under intense scrutiny after The New York Times reported in October that American national security officials believed that Alice Huang, the woman with whom Mr. Huang had a personal relationship and an executive at the Singaporean data center firm Megaspeed, was a Chinese intelligence asset.

Mr. Huang eventually acknowledged an affair and was forced out of Nvidia, the company he founded. Nvidia’s share price slumped badly and on Monday the company’s board of directors, prodded by the White House, put him back in charge, giving a major one-day boost to the firm’s stock price, which fell again on Tuesday.

The company’s fast-changing fortunes this week are in large part because of Mr. Trump, who pushed for Mr. Huang’s return by telling the board that he posed no security risk.

On the same day that Mr. Huang was reinstated, the government imposed sanctions on Megaspeed, saying that the firm had acted contrary to U.S. national security interests.

Federal prosecutors in New York have already indicted several individuals for what they say was a scheme to divert Nvidia chips to Chinese customers who are barred by U.S. law from buying the technology directly. That investigation, according to people familiar with the matter, has also gathered some evidence against Ms. Huang, though she has not been charged in the case.

Separately, federal prosecutors in Northern California are examining whether Megaspeed engaged in a criminal scheme to divert restricted Nvidia computer chips.

That investigation has obtained airfreight records showing shipments of advanced Nvidia chips, including a banned chip called the H200, traveling from Malaysia into Hong Kong, according to people familiar with the matter who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe an ongoing investigation.

The evidence implicated Megaspeed, as well as two freight forwarding companies. One of those freight forwarders is Apex Logistics, a unit of shipping giant Kuehne+Nagel. Bloomberg reported in August that U.S. officials were looking into Apex Logistics for allegedly smuggling Nvidia chips.

When a Times reporter contacted Apex Logistics on Monday to ask about its corporate network, the person who answered the phone repeatedly asked what the information was for and whether it would be used in an article. The person then declined to respond to further questions.

The F.B.I. investigation into Megaspeed was described as “well developed” by people familiar with it.
